title: DRI-MAS
subtitle: A LangGraph multi-agent system that turns plain-English data requests into validated Trino SQL, with four human-in-the-loop interrupts and resumable state.
problem: Analysts spent hours turning business questions into SQL and Excel reports. Each request meant finding the right tables in a large warehouse, resolving company, location, and vertical names across millions of records, writing the query, and checking it by hand. A single LLM prompt could not do this reliably: it guessed table names, merged different companies, and gave no way for a person to step in when it was unsure.

steps.title: A request in plain English
steps.body: Requests arrive from a CLI, a FastAPI service, or a batch CSV. Attachments (CSV, Excel, PDF) are parsed and personal data is masked before any model sees the text.

steps.title: Intent, with a confidence gate
steps.body: The intent agent extracts the entities and metrics being asked for. When its confidence is below the threshold, the graph interrupts and asks a person to clarify; the checkpointer saves state so the run resumes exactly where it stopped.

steps.title: A manager agent plans the work
steps.body: The manager agent reads a corpus of agent and tool specs and writes a typed task plan: which subgraphs to run and in what order. Plans are cached by request type, so repeat requests skip the planning call.

steps.title: Entities fan out by type
steps.body: The normalize subgraph splits the request into companies, locations, and verticals and routes each to its own normalizer. Companies are batched and fanned out per chunk, each resolved with hybrid FAISS + BM25 retrieval over 2.6M company records.

steps.title: Ambiguity goes to a person
steps.body: Results are merged and checked for ambiguous matches. A name that could be two different companies interrupts the graph for a human choice instead of silently picking one.

steps.title: The schema comes from a knowledge graph
steps.body: A schema knowledge graph of tables, fields, join paths, and semantic tags is loaded once per process. An LLM selects the relevant schema, the table selector resolves tables and join paths, and a DDL snippet is built for the SQL step. No match means a human interrupt, not a guess.

steps.title: SQL is generated, then distrusted
steps.body: The SQL generator writes Trino SQL with the canonical names injected, using a query cache keyed by SQL hash. A validator allows SELECT only and rejects blocked keywords, and a dry run confirms every table exists before anything executes.

steps.title: Invalid SQL is reviewed or retried
steps.body: If validation fails, the graph interrupts for review and can loop back to the generator with the error, instead of returning a broken query.

steps.title: A typed result, in under a minute
steps.body: The assemble step returns a typed result with status (success, partial, or failed), the deliverable queries, and which steps completed, failed, or were skipped. Analyst turnaround went from hours to under a minute.

deepDive.heading: State you can stop and resume
deepDive.body: Every stage reads and writes one typed graph state, and every stage result is a Pydantic v2 model, so a malformed output fails at the boundary instead of three steps later.
points: Typed state with merge reducers, so parallel branches combine cleanly
A SQLite checkpointer persists state across interrupt and resume cycles
Each run records completed, failed, and skipped steps in the final result

deepDive.heading: Four places a person can step in
deepDive.body: Human review sits where a wrong answer is expensive, not everywhere.
points: Intent: confidence below threshold
Normalize: an entity matches more than one record
Schema: no schema matches the request
SQL: the generated query fails validation

deepDive.heading: Batch mode for bulk requests
deepDive.body: The same graph runs over a CSV of requests. Batch mode turns off every interrupt; an error is recorded, the row is marked failed, and processing continues with the next row.
points: One failing request never stops the batch
A batch abort skips the remaining steps for that row

deepDive.heading: Memory, caching, and routing
deepDive.body: Repeated work is cached at three levels, and each stage can use a different model.
points: Plan memory keyed by request type
Query memory keyed by SQL hash
The schema knowledge graph loads once per process
Per-stage model routing for intent, schema, and SQL generation
Per-agent call statistics saved per session

deepDive.heading: Read-only by construction
deepDive.body: The SQL path is built so a bad query cannot change data: SELECT-only validation, a keyword blocklist, and a dry run that checks table existence. The deliverable is the validated query set, marked as dry-run.

decisions: A manager agent over three subgraphs instead of one prompt, so normalization, schema selection, and SQL generation are each tested and evaluated on their own.
Hybrid FAISS + BM25 for entity names: semantic search handles paraphrase, BM25 keeps exact names and acronyms from drifting.
Interrupts plus a checkpointer instead of full autonomy: a person resolves the four expensive failure modes and the run resumes without starting over.
Batch mode trades interactivity for throughput: no interrupts, failures recorded per row.

title: Company Synonym Agent
subtitle: Entity resolution for company names across 2.67M company and subsidiary records: semantic recall, lexical rescoring, rule boosts, and an LLM plus a person only for the hard cases.
problem: The same company shows up as an acronym, a spelling variant, a legal-suffix variant, or one of its subsidiaries, depending on the dataset. That breaks joins and every SQL query built on them. Exact matching misses real matches; loose fuzzy matching merges companies that are different.

steps.title: Clean the name, keep the acronym
steps.body: Names are normalized and legal suffixes stripped. Multi-word names also get an acronym token, so a short form can match the full name.

steps.title: Semantic recall over 2.67M records
steps.body: All queries in a batch are embedded at once and searched against a FAISS index of about 2.67M company and subsidiary records. Candidates are over-fetched at ten times top-k, at least 50, so the lexical step has room to work.

steps.title: Lexical rescoring, only where it matters
steps.body: BM25 runs over the semantic candidates rather than the whole corpus, which keeps lexical scoring cheap at this scale. Ineligible records drop out, and the score is 0.6 semantic plus 0.4 normalized BM25.

steps.title: Rules for what embeddings miss
steps.body: Fixed boosts cover the cases embeddings get wrong: an exact clean match (+0.3), a prefix match (+0.15), the query equal to the candidate's acronym (+0.5), and the parent name contained in the candidate (+0.2).

steps.title: Hierarchy-aware selection
steps.body: A master record within 0.20 of the top score is promoted to first place, and a winning subsidiary is rolled up to its parent company.

steps.title: Escalate only the hard cases
steps.body: A score of 0.85 or more is accepted without any model call. Below that, an LLM decision agent chooses among the candidates, and when the top two stay within 0.05 of each other the pipeline pauses for a person.

results.label: Score accepted without an LLM call

deepDive.heading: Recall wide, score narrow
deepDive.body: Semantic search is good at recall and bad at exact names; BM25 is the opposite. Running BM25 only over the semantic candidates gets both without scoring 2.67M documents lexically on every query.

deepDive.heading: An escalation ladder
deepDive.body: Cost and auditability go together: most names resolve with arithmetic, some need a model, a few need a person.
points: Score ≥ 0.85: accepted, no model call
Fuzzy or no match: an LLM chooses among the retrieved candidates
Top two within 0.05: paused for a human decision

deepDive.heading: From library to service
deepDive.body: The engine was later extracted into a standalone service (dense HNSW vectors plus sparse BM25 behind FastAPI), so the multi-agent app no longer loads the embedding stack and degrades to a stub when the service is down.

decisions: Semantic recall over the full corpus, BM25 only on the candidates: cheap lexical precision at 2.67M scale.
Explicit acronym and parent boosts instead of hoping embeddings learn them.
The LLM sees only below-threshold cases and only chooses among retrieved candidates, so it cannot invent a company.

title: Deal Origination Framework (DOF)
subtitle: A weekly business-signal pipeline for 537 enterprise accounts: collect from newsrooms and news, deduplicate syndicated copies, classify each event once, and rank the top two per vertical.
problem: Every week a deal-origination team has to spot business signals (leadership changes, partnerships, acquisitions, investments) across hundreds of enterprise accounts, then pick the strongest two per industry vertical for a dashboard and a deck. By hand that means visiting every newsroom, searching the news, throwing away syndicated copies of the same story, and judging relevance one article at a time.

steps.title: A fixed weekly window
steps.body: Each run loads the account list and the signal taxonomy and computes the previous Monday to Sunday in one timezone. Discovery looks back 14 days so late-listed releases are still caught; a late item is tagged, never dropped.

steps.title: Fan out per account
steps.body: Every account gets a newsroom-discovery task and a news-search task in a persistent SQLite queue that workers claim atomically. Newsroom discovery diffs links against a cumulative URL inventory, so only new URLs move on; news-search links are decoded to the real publisher URL.

steps.title: Fetch once, date carefully
steps.body: All fetches share a pool of at most four long-lived browsers, and HTML or PDF becomes Markdown. The publication date comes from a nine-step ladder, from structured data down to an LLM as the last resort, and every date records its source and confidence.

steps.title: Validate without deleting
steps.body: Each document gets a window status (in window, outside, unknown date, late arrival) and a company-match check. Rejections are kept as statuses rather than deleted, and a barrier waits for every collect task before moving on.

steps.title: Syndicated copies become one event
steps.body: Four dedup layers run per account: canonical URL, content hash, title similarity, and near-duplicate content. Union-find then merges syndicated copies into a single event, with the official release as the canonical document.

steps.title: One LLM call per event
steps.body: The model is called once per event, not per article: ten copies of a story cost one call. A single response carries relevance, vertical, signal strength, a summary, verbatim evidence, and confidence, validated against the taxonomy with one repair turn and one fresh retry.

steps.title: Uncertain events go to an analyst
steps.body: Low confidence, a vertical mismatch, or a failed validation sends the event to review. Analysts work in an exported spreadsheet with taxonomy dropdowns, and importing their decisions rebuilds the ranking.

steps.title: Rank, report, and prove it
steps.body: A deterministic sort picks the top two per vertical (strength, confidence, source count, official source, recency), at most one per account. Reports are written atomically, and a run is only marked complete when report row counts match the database.

results.label: LLM call per event, however many copies

deepDive.heading: Deterministic first
deepDive.body: The model is used only for semantic judgement: relevance, vertical, strength, and evidence. Dates, deduplication, clustering, and ranking are plain code, so they are fast, testable, and identical on every run.

deepDive.heading: No silent data loss, no false done
deepDive.body: Phases are separated by barriers, every result is persisted as soon as it exists, and runs can pause and resume.
points: Rejected documents become statuses, never deletions
A reconciliation mismatch marks the run FAILED instead of complete

deepDive.heading: A real-data validation run
deepDive.body: A one-week run over the first 20 accounts produced 591 tasks (569 succeeded, 22 failed), 383 documents, and 27 events, and reconciliation passed. That run stubbed the classifier, so it validates collection through clustering, not classification quality.

deepDive.heading: Browsers as a fixed pool
deepDive.body: A browser per page was rejected for cost, and multi-tab control would have depended on undocumented driver internals. A pool of at most four long-lived browsers, one per worker, keeps fetching predictable.

decisions: Classify events, not articles: syndicated copies collapse first, so the model sees each story once.
The taxonomy is enforced by a validator, never trusted from the model output.
Analyst review happens in a spreadsheet the team already uses, with dropdowns generated from the taxonomy.

title: Skill Proficiency Engine
subtitle: Tags every skill in a job description with one of five proficiency levels, backed by a quote from the JD, and answers 'not stated' instead of guessing.
problem: Job descriptions list skills but rarely say how good someone needs to be at each one. An LLM asked to fill that gap will produce a confident level for every skill, including the ones the JD never mentions. The engine has to tag each mapped skill with one of five levels, Beginner to Master, and every level has to be backed by text in the JD.

steps.title: Assemble, then check the cache
steps.body: Inputs are rebuilt from confirmed fields only. A cache keyed on the JD, the skill, the model, and the prompt and rubric version skips anything already resolved.

steps.title: Explicit evidence before any model
steps.body: The engine finds the sentence that mentions the skill, then tries a years-of-experience pattern and a level-keyed phrase and verb lexicon. Evidence found this way skips the LLM entirely and is never overridden later.

steps.title: Batched proposals, with a quote
steps.body: Only unresolved skills reach the model, ten at a time. Every proposed level must come with a quote from the JD or it is rejected, and a failing batch is retried and then split in half down to single skills.

steps.title: One place to standardize
steps.body: Every raw signal, whether years, a phrase, a verb, or a model label, maps to one of five canonical levels in a single function.

steps.title: Verify the quote twice
steps.body: Every entry gets a mechanical check that its quote really appears in the JD. Entries that came from the model also get a narrow second call that asks only whether the quote supports the level.

steps.title: Exactly one entry per skill
steps.body: Every input skill ends with one entry recording how it was resolved: years, phrase, verb, or LLM-verified. A failed check becomes NOT_STATED rather than a guessed level.

results.label: Skills per LLM batch, bisected on failure

deepDive.heading: 'Not stated' is a valid answer
deepDive.body: Most proficiency tools always return a level. This one treats missing evidence as an outcome, so downstream analysis can tell 'the JD asks for expert Python' apart from 'the JD mentions Python'.

deepDive.heading: Two layers against hallucination
deepDive.body: A quote is mandatory, the quote must be a substring of the JD, and a second model call must agree that the quote supports the level. Any failure ends in NOT_STATED.

deepDive.heading: Scope kept small on purpose
deepDive.body: The first version made one call per skill. This version resolves what it can without a model, batches the rest, and defers cross-JD comparison to a separate later stage instead of building it in.

decisions: Deterministic evidence first, and the model can never override it.
Bisect-on-failure batching, so one bad skill does not sink the other nine.
A single function maps every signal to the five levels, so the rubric lives in one place.

title: Invoice-to-PO Decision Workflow
subtitle: An accounts-payable workflow where AI reads, code decides, and people own the exceptions: every invoice ends as approve, hold with one question, or reject, and every check cites its source record.
problem: Accounts payable has to match each invoice against its purchase order, goods receipt, and vendor master, and catch duplicates, bank-change fraud, and GST errors. A model that approves payments is a liability, and one that can be talked into approving by text inside the invoice is worse.

steps.title: Any format in, processed once
steps.body: Text PDFs go through pdftotext and scans through OCR. Row totals, subtotal, and grand total are cross-checked, so OCR digit errors are caught without a model, and an idempotency key means a resent invoice is processed once.

steps.title: A queue that fails closed
steps.body: A database-backed queue claims each job, retries with backoff up to three times, and turns a system error into HOLD. Nothing approves by accident.

steps.title: Checks against the systems of record
steps.body: Intake scans for injected instructions, then each check writes evidence of expected versus actual: arithmetic, vendor and bank details, and the PO. It catches a PO edited after the invoice date, a recently changed bank account, and a cancelled GSTIN.

steps.title: Three-way match and GST
steps.body: Price is checked against the PO and the rate contract, quantity against cumulative goods receipts (which catches split-PO overruns), and the GST head against supplier and buyer state. Credit notes skip the match.

steps.title: The model advises, rules decide
steps.body: A TypeSafe Jev decision model judges likely duplicates and suggests a PO, but an action allow-list drops anything it says except an added HOLD. The most severe finding wins, and approval needs confidence of at least 0.85.

steps.title: One question for one person
steps.body: Every HOLD carries a named owner, a next step, and a draft email to the vendor (except suspected bank fraud, which gets no draft). Every check is cited in the evidence trail.

steps.title: Evaluation as a gate
steps.body: One offline command runs every eval suite, and CI runs it on every change with recorded model answers, so no secrets are needed. A regression below the gate fails the build.

results.label: Prompt-injection attacks that changed a decision

decisions: AI reads, code decides, people own the exceptions.
Fail closed plus idempotency instead of best-effort processing.
Gate the judge only on what its own meta-evaluation supports.

deepDive.heading: The model may only add caution
deepDive.body: Model output passes through an action allow-list: the only thing it can contribute to a decision is an extra HOLD. Approval is a deterministic rule outcome with a confidence floor of 0.85.

deepDive.heading: Fail closed, everywhere
deepDive.body: System errors become HOLD, a resent invoice is idempotent, and the queue gives up after three tries into HOLD rather than dropping the job.

deepDive.heading: A judge that is itself evaluated
deepDive.body: The LLM-as-judge was checked against a 69-item human-labelled gold set (kappa 0.659, bad-item recall 1.0). It is only allowed to gate on criteria that passed that meta-evaluation; the explanation criteria failed it, so they stay advisory.

deepDive.heading: Free to run, free to deploy
deepDive.body: Replay mode serves recorded model answers by default, so CI and the free Render deployment need no API key, and the whole eval suite costs nothing to rerun.

title: Finn Advisor
subtitle: A single-user financial assistant over read-only brokerage data, where every number comes from code and the LLM only explains it.
problem: An assistant connected to a brokerage account should answer 'how is my portfolio doing, why did this fall, am I over-concentrated' from real holdings and live news. It must never trade, leak tokens, invent numbers, or follow instructions buried in web content.

steps.title: A safety gate with no model in it
steps.body: Regular-expression rules refuse prompt injection, credential requests, and questions about other people's data before any LLM or tool runs.

steps.title: Deterministic routing
steps.body: Intent is matched in code and sent to a LangGraph workflow: portfolio or research. Only questions the router cannot place go to a Google ADK agent with four sub-agents.

steps.title: Memory, then a degradable login
steps.body: Long-term memory loads with privacy levels and writes only after the user confirms. If the brokerage login has expired, the workflow takes a degraded branch instead of failing.

steps.title: Read-only by policy
steps.body: The brokerage is reached over MCP, with its tools loaded as LangChain tools. An allow-list admits 16 read-only tools; trading tools and anything unknown are blocked inside the client.

steps.title: Numbers come from code
steps.body: Allocation, concentration, and risk are computed without a model, and every section of the snapshot is tagged with where it came from: brokerage data, web search, or a deterministic calculation.

steps.title: Web results are data, not instructions
steps.body: Research questions search the web with a fallback provider, and results are fenced as untrusted external data before they reach the model.

steps.title: Explain, log, and check the output
steps.body: The LLM router falls back from NVIDIA NIM to Gemini Flash and logs every call with the reason for any fallback. The model only explains numbers it was given, and a final check withholds anything that looks like a leaked secret.

results.label: LLM calls in the input safety gate

decisions: Route in code; use the ADK agent only as a fallback for unmatched questions.
Enforce read-only access in the tool policy, not the prompt.
Treat a failed brokerage login as a degraded answer, not an error.

deepDive.heading: The LLM explains, never calculates
deepDive.body: Every figure in an answer was computed in code and carries a provenance tag, so a number can be traced to brokerage data, a search result, or a calculation, and the model has nothing to invent.

deepDive.heading: Safety as code, with honest limits
deepDive.body: Injection and credential requests are blocked by rules, write tools by the MCP tool policy, and leaked secrets by an output screen.
points: Buy and sell advice is limited only by the system prompt
Web content is fenced as data, but not scanned for instructions
The offline eval set has 4 cases and the red-team suite 10, run through a mock evaluator

deepDive.heading: Room to grow into A2A
deepDive.body: The ADK agent calls LangGraph workflows directly in Python, behind an interface that can later become an agent-to-agent call without changing the workflows.

title: ChunkLab
subtitle: A Streamlit lab for comparing chunking, retrieval, and reranking strategies side by side, scored with standard IR metrics on a built-in labelled set.
problem: RAG quality is decided before the model sees anything: by how text is chunked, embedded, retrieved, and reranked. Those choices are usually made by habit, and the effect of changing one is rarely measured.

steps.title: A registry per stage
steps.body: Every strategy registers itself with a decorator, and a duplicate name raises an error. Adding a technique is one new file, and it shows up in every comparison for its stage.

steps.title: Messy files to clean text
steps.body: Uploads are converted to Markdown with LiteParse, or cleaned with Chonkie's text, Markdown, and table preprocessors.

steps.title: Eleven ways to cut a document
steps.body: Character, recursive, token, semantic, embedding-semantic, Markdown, table, and tree-sitter code splitting, plus three Chonkie chunkers, each with its boundaries drawn on the text.

steps.title: Seven retrievers on the same documents
steps.body: Keyword, boolean, TF-IDF, BM25, dense, hybrid, and MMR rank the same pasted documents. Hybrid fuses BM25 and dense results with reciprocal rank fusion.

steps.title: Rerank, then prove it helped
steps.body: Six rerankers run on the candidates, and MRR and NDCG are compared before and after reranking on the built-in labelled set.

steps.title: One yardstick per stage
steps.body: Embeddings get intrinsic evals (Spearman correlation, analogies, clustering ARI); retrieval gets P@k, R@k, MRR, MAP, and NDCG. The Metrics Explorer names the best strategy per metric, and every run is logged with its latency.

decisions: Self-registering plugins with a duplicate-name check, so the registry stays the single list of strategies.
Deterministic, model-free approximations for speed and reproducibility, disclosed rather than hidden.

deepDive.heading: What is real and what is simulated
deepDive.body: The lab runs with no model downloads, which means two components are approximations, said plainly:
points: The 'dense' retriever uses a 64-dimension hash embedding, not a neural model
The cross-encoder reranker is simulated
IR metrics run on a built-in set of 6 documents and 3 queries, not on your own documents

deepDive.heading: Comparisons within a stage
deepDive.body: Each page compares strategies for one stage at a time. Retrieval works on pasted documents rather than the chunker's output, so the lab answers 'which retriever is best here', not 'which full pipeline is best'.

title: Instagram MCP Server
subtitle: An MCP server that gives Claude and ChatGPT 36 allow-listed Instagram actions through Composio, built to keep working when OAuth is unfinished or the upstream is down.
problem: Claude and ChatGPT cannot act on an Instagram Business account (posts, carousels, comments, DMs, insights) without Graph API OAuth and glue code for every endpoint. The server has to expose those actions safely, on a serverless runtime with a read-only filesystem, and stay usable when the OAuth connection is not finished.

steps.title: One HTTP endpoint
steps.body: FastMCP serves the MCP protocol over streamable HTTP on the port the serverless runtime provides.

steps.title: OAuth that does not block startup
steps.body: If the Instagram account is not connected yet, the server starts the OAuth flow, logs the redirect URL, and waits up to five minutes. On timeout it boots anyway, so the utility tools still work.

steps.title: Tool schemas discovered at runtime
steps.body: A low-level list_tools handler maps Composio's JSON schemas straight into MCP tools, limited to an allow-list of 36 actions. If discovery fails, the last known list is served from cache.

steps.title: Writes are never retried
steps.body: Any tool name that is not a utility passes through as a Composio action. Discovery retries with backoff, but writes do not: retrying after an unclear error could publish the same post twice.

steps.title: Errors as results, not crashes
steps.body: Every exception comes back as an MCP error result instead of breaking the session, and each call is counted in per-tool stats exposed by the health tool.

deepDive.heading: Why low-level handlers
deepDive.body: Decorator-based tools need their schemas at import time. Here the schemas only exist after Composio discovery, so the server implements list_tools and call_tool directly and maps schemas on the fly.

deepDive.heading: Built for a read-only sandbox
deepDive.body: The serverless runtime ignores the Dockerfile and mounts a read-only home directory, so anything the server writes goes to a temporary directory and falls back to memory if that fails too.

deepDive.heading: The allow-list is the security boundary
deepDive.body: Both the Composio session and discovery are limited to the same 36 actions, so a client cannot reach an Instagram endpoint that was not deliberately exposed.

decisions: Retry reads, never writes.
Boot with partial capability rather than fail when OAuth is incomplete.
One allow-list shared by session and discovery.

title: Outlook CLI
subtitle: An npm CLI and stdio MCP server for Outlook mail and calendar over Microsoft Graph: one OAuth login, one tool registry shared by humans and agents.
problem: Managing Outlook from a terminal or an agent usually means an OAuth dance on every run and output written only for humans. The tool needed one login, reusable tokens, and output an agent can parse, with the same behaviour whether a person or an assistant is calling it.

steps.title: Two front doors, one behaviour
steps.body: The terminal CLI and the stdio MCP server both call the same frozen tool registry, so a command and the matching agent tool cannot drift apart.

steps.title: Log in once
steps.body: The first call opens a delegated-permission OAuth flow in the browser and saves the tokens locally. Every later call reuses them and refreshes them when they expire.

steps.title: 21 tools across four domains
steps.body: Mail (including attachments), calendar, folders, and inbox rules, each a handler behind the shared registry.

steps.title: Graph, or a mock
steps.body: Every request goes through one Graph client, and a test-mode switch swaps in mock data so the suite runs without an account.

steps.title: Output for people and for agents
steps.body: The CLI renders themed tables for people and switches to machine-readable output with --json or --ai.

deepDive.heading: Built on an existing server
deepDive.body: The project extends the open-source ryaker/outlook-mcp server. The additions here are the CLI front end, the shared tool registry, attachment handling, the jest test suite, and npm packaging.

deepDive.heading: Publishing with checks
deepDive.body: Publishing runs the test suite and a dry-run pack first, so a broken build or a missing file never reaches npm.

decisions: One registry for both interfaces, so humans and agents get identical behaviour.
Machine-readable output as a first-class mode, not an afterthought.
A deliberately small dependency surface: the MCP SDK, chalk, and dotenv.
